title: How can a wallet backup become a list of words?
dek: Twelve ordinary words can stand in for 128 random bits. There is no encryption involved, just counting, a small checksum and a list of 2,048 words.

blocks.text: Many wallets ask you to record a list of 12 or 24 words and keep it secret. This list is a *mnemonic phrase*. BIP 39 uses it to encode computer-generated randomness in a form that people can write on paper or read aloud. The user does not invent the words as a password.

The proposal, assigned in 2013 and recorded as deployed, has two halves: turning random bits into words, and turning words into a binary seed for later wallet machinery. This chapter follows both, using only published test phrases that anyone can look up, and values computed from them.

figure.title: A published test phrase
figure.caption: Each word stands for a number from 0 to 2,047. The numbers carry the entropy and its checksum, but the seed is later computed from the words themselves.

blocks.text: The starting value is entropy: random bits produced by a computer. BIP 39 allows between 128 and 256 bits, in steps of 32. More random bits increase resistance to guessing and require a longer mnemonic phrase.

Why words at all? A 128-bit number written in hexadecimal is thirty-two characters of digits and letters, easy to transpose and tiring to read aloud. Twelve familiar words carry the same information in a form that is easier to copy by hand and to check against the original.

blocks.title: 128 random bits
blocks.caption: The entropy of a published sample, bit by bit and as hexadecimal.

blocks.text: The proposal is explicit that it transcribes randomness. It is not a way to turn a sentence someone made up into a wallet; such *brainwallets* are outside its scope.

Before any words appear, the entropy gets a short checksum. Hash the entropy with SHA-256 and keep the first ENT / 32 bits of the result, where ENT is the number of entropy bits: 4 checksum bits for 128 bits of entropy, 8 for 256. Append them to the end.

The total is now a multiple of 11: 132 bits for 128 bits of entropy, 264 for 256. Cut it into 11-bit groups. Each group is a number from 0 to 2,047, and each number picks one word from a list of exactly 2,048. Twelve groups give twelve words; twenty-four give twenty-four.

The published all-zero sample shows the whole procedure at its plainest. Its 128 entropy bits are all zero. The SHA-256 hash of those sixteen zero bytes happens to begin with the bits `0011`, so those four bits become the checksum. The first eleven groups are eleven zeros each, index 0, the word *abandon*. The last group is seven zeros followed by `0011`: index 3, the word *about*. That is why this famous test phrase reads *abandon* eleven times and then *about*. All-zero entropy is, of course, useless as a real backup: it is public precisely because it is predictable.

blocks.title: Making the checksum
blocks.caption: The all-zero sample: its hash begins with the bits 0011, which become the checksum.

blocks.text: The figure below starts from the bits of a public sample. Move the slider to cut them into groups of 11 and watch each group pick its word.

blocks.title: From bits to words
blocks.caption: The last word is not “the checksum word”. In a 12-word phrase it carries 7 bits of entropy and 4 checksum bits; in a 24-word phrase, 3 and 8.
The first four columns are BIP 39’s own table. The last follows from appending the checksum after the entropy.

blocks.text: Leading zeros count. The 24-word sample beginning *all hour* comes from entropy whose first five bits are zero, and those zeros are part of its first group like any other bits.

The list has 2,048 words for a reason: 2,048 is two to the eleventh power, so every word stands for exactly 11 bits, no more and no less. The mnemonic phrase therefore represents all the bits in the entropy and checksum.

blocks.title: Eleven bits, one word
blocks.caption: Every 11-bit number has exactly one card in a list of 2,048.

blocks.text: BIP 39 describes the properties of an ideal wordlist. The first four letters should identify each word. Similar pairs such as *build* and *built* or *woman* and *women* should be avoided. Sorting the list lets software search it quickly.

The pinned English list used on this page has 2,048 entries, and the tests behind it confirm that no two share their first four letters. Lists with accented or composed characters must be stored in a Unicode form called NFKD, a detail that returns below.
Wordlists exist in other languages. BIP 39 strongly discourages generating mnemonic phrases from them because most wallets support only the English list.

A checksum lets software notice a wrong word, but this one is small. BIP 39 lists it among its own shortcomings: it gives only modest odds of catching random errors, citing one in 256 missed, and offers no help correcting them.

That figure matches the 8 checksum bits of a 24-word phrase. A 12-word phrase has only 4, so swapping its last word for a random one still passes one time in sixteen. The tests behind this page count exactly 128 of the 2,048 possible last words that do.

blocks.title: One last word in sixteen
blocks.caption: Keep the first eleven words and try every possible last word: the filled cells pass the checksum.

blocks.text: BIP 39 requires software to compute the mnemonic phrase’s checksum and warn if it is invalid. The checksum does not identify the incorrect word.

Seed derivation uses the mnemonic phrase directly. It does not first recover the original entropy. BIP 39 applies PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512, 2,048 iterations and a 64-byte result. The mnemonic phrase supplies the password input. The salt is the word `mnemonic` followed by an optional passphrase. Both inputs are normalized to NFKD first.

The result is 512 bits, four times the 128 bits of entropy behind a 12-word phrase, yet it holds no new randomness. Every bit of it is fixed by the words and the passphrase. A wallet that never asks for a passphrase is simply using the empty one.

blocks.title: Words and passphrase to seed
blocks.caption: The published vector’s passphrase is “TREZOR”. Change it, or leave it empty, and the seed changes completely: see the next section.

blocks.text: The seed depends on the mnemonic phrase’s text, not just the entropy it represents. Encoding the same entropy with a different wordlist produces a different seed. Seed derivation provides no way to recover the mnemonic phrase from the seed.

Unicode can write some visible text in more than one way. NFKD picks one decomposed form, so that two devices showing the same characters feed the same bytes into PBKDF2. The Japanese test vectors referenced by BIP 39 use passphrases full of symbols such as ㍍, which NFKD expands into the four characters メートル. The tests behind this page check all 24 of those vectors.

The seed-derivation step does not check the checksum or require a particular phrase structure. Clients can use their own wordlists or sentence generators. However, BIP 39 advises against phrases that its encoding algorithm did not produce. Software must still compute the checksum with a wordlist and warn if it is invalid.

The optional passphrase changes the seed entirely, and every passphrase produces a valid one. BIP 39 presents this as plausible deniability: only the right passphrase opens the intended wallet, while any other opens a different, working wallet rather than an error.

blocks.title: Same words, two passphrases
blocks.caption: Neither seed is wrong: each passphrase simply leads to its own wallet.

blocks.text: An app’s unlock password protects a local wallet file, and the app can report an incorrect password. A mistyped BIP 39 passphrase can instead produce a different valid seed. Seed derivation does not report a passphrase error. The resulting wallet may therefore differ from the one the user intended.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: A mnemonic is not a private key, but together with its passphrase, if any, it is everything needed to rebuild the keys. Anyone who sees both can recreate the wallet. This page never asks for a phrase and only shows published test vectors and values computed from them.
The 64-byte seed is input for key derivation, not a signing key. BIP 32 or a similar scheme derives the wallet’s keys from it. The next chapter explains that step.

The mnemonic phrase encodes entropy. Seed derivation uses that phrase and the optional passphrase. Key derivation then uses the seed. The phrase and its passphrase, if used, can reproduce the seed and keys. The seed alone can reproduce the keys. Keep all this secret material private.

blocks.title: Still not a key
blocks.caption: Encoding represents entropy as a mnemonic phrase. Seed derivation uses the phrase and the passphrase. The next chapter explains key derivation from the seed.

blocks.text: BIP 39 lists other shortcomings too, including the lack of a versioning scheme, which it notes is now largely mitigated by descriptor wallets. Its authors proposed a scheme called SLIP-0039 as an intended successor.
